chapter_title: Also concerning the Catechumen; shall he be saved in a single Body?
chapter_note: This chapter is overwhelmingly institutional/pastoral (catechumen discipline, merit accounting, church protection) wrapped in dialogue frame. Only brief fragments preserve older-looking cosmological soteriology (post-mortem ascent/purification; formation of a “light image”). A clear NT/Pauline overlay appears in the quotation about wives/buying/rejoicing (1 Cor 7), and a likely Gospel proverb appears at the end of the purification sequence (Mt 6:21).

paragraphs.temporal_note: Dialogue frame (“Once again… speaks… to this apostle”) presenting the topic; catechumen category anchors it to church life.
Petition formula (“Now I beseech you… my master”) and didactic intent (“instruct my other brothers… proclaim it to the catechumens”) mark editorial framing/institutional use.
Household/sexual renunciation and orientation to “the holy church” describes idealized catechumen conduct; not cosmos→cosmos mapping but social-ethical application.
Explicit appeal to “the saviour” and a Pauline-style citation (“let these who have wives be like…”) indicates NT entry-vector (1 Cor 7).
Seam-like summary applying the preceding to “perfect catechumens… like the elect”; institutional extension rather than substrate.
Fasting/prayer/alms and repeated “holy church / elect / wife / children” language is institutional discipline, not systematic cosmology.
Institutional encouragement plus internal book reference (“Treasure of Life”) and catechumen typology; not substrate.

paragraphs.core_text: When, however, they come forth from their body, they travel on their way and pass by in the place above, and go in to the life. They shall be purified in the heavens, and they are plucked just as a fruit that ripens is plucked from the tree.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the subsequent institutional application: the alms-offering to the elect and the explicit comparison “Similarly, the souls of the catechumens…”; this shifts from ascent/purification mechanics to church practice (cosmos→institution).
paragraphs.temporal_note: Opening lines present impersonal ascent/purification mechanics with a natural correspondence (fruit-plucking). The paragraph then pivots to alms-to-elect application, a later institutional graft.
Appeal to “Treasure of Life” and purification “in accordance with… contribution to the church” is institutional accounting.
Prescriptive repentance/forgiveness via “God and the holy church” and bookkeeping of sins (“first and the last”) is pastoral/institutional.
Closing praise scene and exalted address (“Blessed are you… our father”) is hagiographic frame.
Extended petition-question (“we beseech you… recount…”) embedded in community concerns about prior sins and sects; functions as editorial Q&A apparatus.

Though it uses Light/Darkness vocabulary, it is cast as church-mediated absolution (“right hand of peace… Light Mind who dwells in the holy church”), i.e., cosmology leveraged for institutional soteriology.
Doctrinal rule of absolution contingent on persistence in belief; anchored to renouncing “sects and idols of error,” not to cosmic system exposition.
Moral/pastoral warning about relapse and retribution; explicit catechumen/elect categories.
Institutional means of absolution (fasting/prayer/alms) stated directly; no cosmological mechanism.
Detailed rule list (fifty fasts, sexual restraint, diet prohibitions) is catechumen discipline.
Hours of prayer, alms counting, garments for saints, “daily communion” style institutional practice language.
Merit arithmetic (“five parts… absolved from four… protection of the holy church… love of the elect”) is explicitly institutional, even if it uses Light/Darkness phrasing.

paragraphs.core_text: ⟨p.234⟩ As for the rest, he shall be questioned about a single part; and receive blows for (those sins) and retribution. Afterwards he is purified, whether indeed above or below. He shall be purified according to the worth of his deeds, and cleansed and washed and adorned. Afterwards, he is sculpted a light image; and [he glid]es up and reaches the land of rest,
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the final Gospel-like proverb clause (“so that the place where his heart is, his treasure also will be there”), likely entering via Mt 6:21; it is not part of the impersonal purification mechanism.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal, process-focused soteriology (purification above/below; formation of a “light image”; ascent to the land of rest) reads like older cosmological teaching; the concluding heart/treasure line is a recognizable NT overlay.
Conditional exhortation about steadfastness and recompense; catechumen perseverance motif.
Moral warning about lying/apostasy and renewed judgement; institutional soteriology.
General promise of destiny/release for steadfast faith; lacks systematic cosmological mapping and remains paraenetic.
Narrative closure (“When these disciples had heard… they gave glory…”) functions as framing doxology despite brief cosmological vocabulary (“first light… Mind”).
